opening_mood.text: Happy Bank Holiday Monday. While the City is largely quiet and the LSE is shut, the global markets haven't taken the day off. We've got a massive geopolitical shift in the Middle East sending oil sliding, a cheeky mega-cap tech land grab in Europe, and Elon Musk filing the biggest S-1 in human history. Grab a flat white (or a pint, seeing as it's a bank holiday) and let's get you prepped for the week ahead.

sections.title: Daily Finance & Business News: Bank Holiday Blockbusters

content.text: Happy Bank Holiday Monday. While the London Stock Exchange and Wall Street are closed today for the Spring Bank Holiday and Memorial Day, the rest of the world has not stopped spinning. In fact, the last 24 hours have delivered some of the most consequential macro and corporate news of the year. Grab a coffee, and let us get you up to speed on what is actually moving the needle.
1. Hormuz Peace Dividend: US-Iran Talks Send Oil Crashing

Over the weekend, President Trump and regional officials signalled that a deal is close to being finalised to end the conflict with Iran. The agreement in principle would end the war, reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and see Iran surrender its highly enriched uranium. In response, Brent crude plummeted over 4%, dropping below $100 a barrel to around $95.52, while WTI fell to $91.86. Global equities surged to record highs, with European airline and travel stocks (like Air France-KLM and Lufthansa) leading the charge on the prospect of lower fuel costs and reopened flight paths.

Why it matters: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has been the single biggest inflationary threat of 2026. Reopening it removes a massive supply-side bottleneck and eases energy costs globally. Macro desks and inflation-sensitive portfolios are rapidly repricing. A drop in oil takes some of the immediate pressure off central banks, although the long-term structural inflation risks remain.

items: What to say at work: "The peace dividend is real, but let's not get ahead of ourselves. A drop in Brent to the mid-90s is great for airlines, but with the Fed still sounding hawkish, is this enough to actually change the rate trajectory?"

content.text: 2. Uber's Cheeky €11.5bn Bid for Delivery Hero

Uber has launched a formal takeover offer for Berlin-based food delivery giant Delivery Hero, valuing the company at roughly €10 billion ($11.6 billion). The opening bid of €33 per share was actually a slight discount to Friday's close, which did not go down well with major shareholders who are holding out for €40+. Uber already owns a 19.5% stake (plus 5.6% in options) and is reportedly considering raising its bid to €38 after being rebuffed. Delivery Hero shares jumped over 10% in European trading on Monday.

Why it matters: This is a massive consolidation play. Uber is trying to box out its chief rival, DoorDash, which has been expanding its European footprint via Wolt. M&A bankers are licking their lips. This shows that despite higher interest rates, mega-cap tech still has the balance sheet strength to fund massive strategic acquisitions. It also highlights how activist pressure and CEO departures (Delivery Hero's co-founder Niklas Östberg is stepping down) leave companies vulnerable to hostile or opportunistic takeovers.

items: What to say at work: "Uber's €33 bid was a classic lowball opening gambit. Now that they're talking about €38 and shareholders want €40, this has all the makings of a classic bidding war. Will DoorDash or Prosus step in to spoil the party?"

content.text: 3. SpaceX's S-1: Mars, Space-Based AI, and a $1.7 Trillion Valuation

SpaceX officially filed its S-1 prospectus with the SEC for a Nasdaq listing under the ticker SPCX, targeting a valuation of $1.7 trillion to $1.75 trillion and aiming to raise up to $75 billion. The listing could happen as early as June 12. The filing reveals that while Starlink is a cash cow (generating $11.4 billion of the company's $18.7 billion revenue in 2025), the overall company lost $4.94 billion last year due to massive capex ($20.7 billion) and AI-related losses ($6.36 billion) from its xAI unit.

Why it matters: This will be the largest IPO in history. The prospectus reads like a sci-fi novel, pitching a $28.5 trillion TAM, space-based AI data centres powered by solar energy, and a 100-year plan to build a civilization of 1 million people on Mars. For quants and tech investors, the integration of xAI and the plan for space-based AI compute is fascinating. But for governance-focused ESG funds, the dual-class share structure—which gives Elon Musk 85.1% of the voting power despite owning 42% of the equity—is a massive red flag.

items: What to say at work: "SpaceX's S-1 is peak galaxy brain. They're pitching a $28.5 trillion TAM and space-based AI data centers, but they lost $4.9 billion last year on $20.7 billion of capex. Are public markets ready to fund Elon's Mars colony, or is this the ultimate test of the AI/space bubble?"

content.text: 4. The Great British Fire Sale: UK M&A Triples to $192 Billion

A rush of foreign bids for UK companies has put Britain on track to outstrip all previous records for dealmaking in 2026. M&A in the country has more than tripled from this time last year to $192 billion so far. Key deals include EQT's £9.4 billion ($12.7 billion) bid for Intertek, bids for Schroders, and Unilever's food unit, as well as Ingredion's offer for Tate & Lyle.

Why it matters: The UK has been trading at a persistent valuation discount compared to US and European peers. Private equity and foreign corporates are taking advantage of cheap FTSE shares and a predictable, tried-and-tested regulatory landscape for takeovers. Investment banking desks in London are having a bumper year after a dry spell. This is a massive validation of the "cheap UK assets" thesis that value managers have been preaching for years.

items: What to say at work: "With UK M&A tripling to $192bn, the FTSE discount is finally being closed by corporate buyers rather than public market re-ratings. Is there any value left in mid-cap UK, or is everything about to be taken private?"

content.text: 5. Fed's Waller Warns: The Easing Bias is Dead

Fed Governor Christopher Waller delivered a hawkish speech arguing that the Fed should remove its "easing bias" from its policy statement and can no longer rule out rate hikes down the road if inflation doesn't ease. This comes as the University of Michigan survey showed a rise in inflation expectations and a drop in consumer sentiment.

Why it matters: This is a significant shift. Markets have been holding onto the hope of rate cuts, but Waller is signalling that the next move could actually be a hike if inflation remains sticky. Fixed income desks are bracing for "higher for longer" or even "higher still." Yields have been climbing.

items: What to say at work: "Waller's comments on removing the easing bias suggest the Fed is genuinely worried about a second wave of inflation. Are we looking at a potential hike by the end of the year if the PCE data next week comes in hot?"

content.text: 6. UK "AI Washing" Backlash

PR executives in the UK are pushing back against companies performing "yoga-level" stretches to describe themselves as AI specialists. Communications firms are complaining that low-tech businesses are demanding to be pitched as AI companies to capitalise on the hype, leading to "AI washing" accusations.

Why it matters: Regulators (like the SEC and FCA) have already warned about AI washing, but this shows the operational reality. Companies are desperate for the "AI premium" in their valuations, even if their tech is just basic automation or a tenuous link. For equity analysts and quants, this is a warning to look under the hood of any company claiming to be an "AI play." The hype is reaching a point of saturation where even PR firms are rolling their eyes.

items: What to say at work: "If even the PR agencies are complaining about 'AI washing', we've officially reached peak hype. How much of the mid-cap tech rally is built on actual LLM integration versus glorified Excel macros?"

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: Friday’s session was a classic "good news is good news" setup, wrapping up an absolute monster of a week for risk assets. The S&P 500 climbed 0.37% to close at 7,473.47, securing its eighth consecutive winning week—the longest such streak since late 2023. Meanwhile, the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.58% to finish at a record 50,579.70. The catalyst? A slight easing in Treasury yields (the 10-year ticked down to 4.56%) and a relief rally in oil, with WTI crude sliding roughly 8% on the week to around $96.44 a barrel. Traders latched onto comments from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio suggesting "good signs" of progress in negotiations to end the US-Israel conflict with Iran and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

But the real theatre of the day wasn't on the trading floor; it was at the White House. Kevin Warsh was officially sworn in as the 17th Chairman of the Federal Reserve, succeeding Jerome Powell. In a move that had Fed watchers choking on their morning macchiatos, Donald Trump handed Warsh the ultimate hall pass during the ceremony, telling him: "I want Kevin to be totally independent... Just do your own thing." For a guy historically viewed as the most hawkish nominee in twenty years—and who has openly called for a "regime change" at the central bank—this is a fascinating setup.

Underneath the hood, the cross-asset picture is screaming that Wall Street and Main Street are living in entirely different dimensions. While equities are partying like it's 1999, the University of Michigan consumer sentiment index collapsed to a record low. Households are getting absolutely battered by sticky inflation and high fuel costs, with short-term inflation expectations rising to 4.8%. This gives Warsh the perfect cover. With headline PCE running at 3.5% and core at 3.2%, the new Fed Chair doesn't actually have to bow to political pressure to cut rates. The data, the hawkish committee, and the bond market are doing the heavy lifting for him, keeping the Fed funds rate firmly paused at 3.75%.

There is also a massive divergence in positioning that quant and macro desks are watching closely. S&P 500 futures touched an all-time high of 7,524, yet the latest CFTC Commitments of Traders report shows large speculators are net short roughly 140,600 E-mini contracts. The equity market is priced for an unstoppable AI capex boom and a swift diplomatic resolution in the Middle East. Meanwhile, the physical crude market (with Brent still carrying a hefty war premium around $105–$110 a barrel) and the bond market are pricing in a much grittier, higher-for-longer reality.

items: Corporate Movers: Ross Stores jumped 8.1% on a stellar earnings beat, while Zoom (+9.2%) and Workday (+5.2%) proved there is still plenty of juice in enterprise tech. Estee Lauder surged 11.9% after calling off its merger talks with Spanish beauty group Puig.

The Yield Curve: The 10-year Treasury yield closed at 4.56%, but the 10-year minus 2-year spread has compressed to exactly 0%, marking the tightest reading of the past year and signalling that the bond market is far from convinced about a soft landing.

The Pub Talk: If you’re chatting with colleagues or clients over a pint, the talking point is Warsh’s "independence". Is Trump’s blessing of autonomy a genuine shift, or a tactical move to distance himself from the political fallout of high interest rates and sticky inflation?

sections.title: Financial Idea of the Day: The Ultimate Free Lunch of Negative Working Capital

content.text: The Ultimate Free Lunch: Negative Working Capital

If you cracked open a standard university corporate finance textbook, you were probably taught that positive working capital is a sign of a healthy, liquid business. The textbook logic is simple: you want your current assets (cash, inventory, receivables) to comfortably exceed your current liabilities (bills due soon) so you do not go bust. But in the real world of high-performance investing, positive working capital is often just a polite term for 'trapped cash'. The real magic happens when a business manages to run on negative working capital.

Negative working capital (specifically, negative operating working capital) occurs when a company's operating liabilities exceed its operating assets. In plain English, it means you collect cash from your customers long before you have to pay your suppliers or deliver your service. Instead of you funding your business, your customers and suppliers are funding it for you—interest-free.
The Math: SaaS vs. Heavy Machinery
To see why this is a cheat code, let's look at two contrasting businesses:

items: Company A (The Cash-Sucker): Sells industrial pumps. It takes 60 days to build a pump (holding inventory), and once delivered, it gives the client 60 days to pay (receivables). Meanwhile, its suppliers demand payment in 30 days. Company A has to find cash from its own pocket to fund this gap. Every time Company A grows, it has to sink more cash into working capital.

Company B (The Cash-Machine): A subscription SaaS business. A customer pays £1,200 upfront for an annual subscription. Company B gets £1,200 cash on day one. On the balance sheet, this is recorded as £1,200 Cash (Asset) and £1,200 Deferred Revenue (Liability). Because Deferred Revenue is an operating liability, Company B's operating working capital is -£1,200. It has £1,200 of free cash to spend on engineering or marketing today, before it has even delivered the service.

content.text: This isn't just a tech thing. Supermarkets like Aldi or Tesco do this brilliantly with physical goods. They sell the milk to you within 2 days of it hitting the shelf (low inventory, instant cash), but they do not pay the dairy farm for 60 days (high payables). They are essentially running their business on a permanent, interest-free loan from their suppliers.
Why Asset Managers Salivate Over It

For an investor, negative working capital does two incredible things. First, it supercharges Free Cash Flow (FCF) during periods of growth. In a standard DCF model, the 'Change in Net Working Capital' is subtracted from operating cash flow. If working capital is negative and the business is growing, that change is a negative number being subtracted—which mathematically becomes an addition to cash flow. Growth actually releases cash.

Second, it breaks the Return on Invested Capital (ROIC) formula in the best way possible. Invested Capital is roughly Net Fixed Assets plus Net Working Capital. If Net Working Capital is deeply negative, the denominator shrinks. This means the business can generate astronomical, sometimes technically infinite, ROIC because it requires virtually no capital of its own to grow.
The Beginner Mistake: Forgetting the Reverse Gear

The classic rookie error is assuming negative working capital is a risk-free perpetual motion machine. It isn't. Negative working capital is highly cyclical and growth-dependent. If a negative working capital business stops growing or starts shrinking, the cash flow dynamic reverses violently. Suddenly, you have to pay off your old suppliers or deliver services to customers who already paid you, but you do not have a fresh wave of new customer cash coming in. The 'float' evaporates, and the business can suffer a sudden, catastrophic liquidity squeeze even if it remains profitable on paper.
How to Use This in Interviews and at Work

You should say: 'It depends entirely on the business model. For a struggling manufacturing firm, negative working capital is a sign of distress and impending insolvency. But for a dominant retailer or a subscription software business, negative working capital is a massive structural advantage. It represents a source of free, non-dilutive funding—essentially a customer-funded float. When the business grows, it generates cash rather than consuming it, which dramatically boosts ROIC. However, the key risk to model is what happens if growth slows down, as the working capital cycle will reverse and drain cash rapidly.'

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day: Path Signatures and the Itô Breakthrough

content.text: Path Signatures and the Itô Breakthrough

If you’ve ever tried to feed a time series into a machine learning model to price an exotic option or generate a trading signal, you’ve probably run into the classic feature-engineering headache. Do you feed it raw prices? Moving averages? Volatility? Or do you throw your hands up and dump the whole lot into a heavy, black-box LSTM that takes three hours to train and overfits if a butterfly flaps its wings in Tokyo?

There is a much more elegant, mathematically rigorous way to do this that has been quietly taking over high-end quant desks: Path Signatures. And a brilliant paper published in Applied Mathematical Finance by Fred Espen Benth, Fabian A. Harang, and Fride Josefine Emberland Straum has just resolved a massive, decades-old theoretical headache that kept signatures from being "technically correct" for real-world finance.
The Idea: What is a Path Signature?

Think of a path signature as a Taylor series expansion, but instead of expanding a single function at a point, it expands an entire path (like a stock price over time). It translates a continuous, messy, infinitely dimensional price path into a neat, finite vector of numbers (iterated integrals) that perfectly describe the "shape" of that path.

The magic of the signature is the Universal Approximation Theorem. It states that any continuous function of a path—whether that’s the payoff of an Asian option, a barrier option, or a complex trading signal—can be approximated to arbitrary precision by a simple linear combination of its signature terms. In plain English: you don't need a deep neural network. You just need a linear regression (or a shallow ridge regression) on the signature of the path.
The Finance Example: Pricing Exotic Options

Let's say you want to price an Asian option, where the payoff depends on the average price of an asset over the last 30 days. Instead of running a million Monte Carlo paths or training a recurrent neural network, you can generate a small set of simulated price paths, compute the path signature for each path up to, say, depth 3, and run a simple linear regression mapping these signature terms to the final option payoff. Because the signature terms capture the average, the variance, and the path's overall trajectory mathematically, the linear model fits almost perfectly.
The 2026 Itô Breakthrough

So, what did Benth, Harang, and Straum actually solve? Historically, the math behind signatures relied on "geometric rough paths," which correspond to Stratonovich integration. But finance doesn't use Stratonovich; we use Itô integration because it preserves the martingale property (which is the bedrock of no-arbitrage pricing). Until recently, quants had to perform awkward mathematical gymnastics—calculating Itô-to-Stratonovich correction terms—to make signatures work without violating no-arbitrage. The authors proved that the Universal Approximation Theorem holds directly on non-geometric rough paths (i.e., Itô space). This means you can use Itô iterated integrals directly as your features, keeping your pricing models mathematically pure and arbitrage-free.
Mini Technical Example: Calculating a Signature in Python

import numpy as np

def compute_simple_signature_2d(prices, times):
    """
    Computes the first and second-order iterated integrals 
    for a 2D path of (Price, Time).
    """
    n = len(prices)
    # First-order terms: simple net changes
    sig_1 = prices[-1] - prices[0]  # Integral of dX
    sig_2 = times[-1] - times[0]    # Integral of dt
    
    # Second-order terms: iterated integrals
    # e.g., Integral of X dt (captures the average price over time)
    sig_12 = 0.0
    # e.g., Integral of t dX (captures when the price moves)
    sig_21 = 0.0
    
    for i in range(1, n):
        dx = prices[i] - prices[i-1]
        dt = times[i] - times[i-1]
        
        # Midpoint approximation for the integrals
        x_mid = 0.5 * (prices[i] + prices[i-1])
        t_mid = 0.5 * (times[i] + times[i-1])
        
        sig_12 += x_mid * dt
        sig_21 += t_mid * dx
        
    return {
        "dX": sig_1, 
        "dt": sig_2, 
        "int_X_dt": sig_12, 
        "int_t_dX": sig_21
    }

# Example: A stock that rallies late vs. rallies early
times = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3])
prices_late = np.array([10, 10, 10, 20])  # Rallies at the end
prices_early = np.array([10, 20, 20, 20]) # Rallies at the start

print("Late Rally:", compute_simple_signature_2d(prices_late, times))
# int_X_dt will be lower because the price stayed low for longer
print("Early Rally:", compute_simple_signature_2d(prices_early, times))
# int_X_dt will be higher because the price stayed high for longer
How to Use This in an Interview or at the Pub

If someone asks you how to model path-dependent features without resorting to heavy, uninterpretable deep learning models, you have the perfect answer: "I’d look at path signatures from rough path theory. They act as a non-parametric feature extractor that maps a continuous path to a finite vector of iterated integrals. Because of the Universal Approximation Theorem, you can approximate any path-dependent payoff or signal using a simple linear model over these signature terms. Plus, a recent paper by Benth, Harang, and Straum in Applied Mathematical Finance finally extended this to non-geometric rough paths. This means we can use Itô iterated integrals directly, keeping our pricing models arbitrage-free without needing annoying Stratonovich corrections."
Risks and Limitations

Before you go and throw signatures at everything, watch out for the curse of dimensionality. The number of terms in a signature grows exponentially with the number of assets (d) and the depth of the truncation (k)—roughly d^k. If you have a portfolio of 50 stocks, even a depth-3 signature gives you 50^3 = 125,000 features, which will instantly overfit a linear regression. You'll need to pair this with dimension reduction techniques, like Kernel Signature methods or PCA, to keep it tractable.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading: The Five Sins of Financial LLMs

content.text: If you spend any time on LinkedIn or reading sell-side research, you have probably been bombarded with pitches about how Large Language Models (LLMs) are the new holy grail of alpha generation. Every second fintech startup claims to have built a 'GPT-powered trading agent' that prints money. But if you have ever tried to put these models into production, you will know that the gap between a backtest and reality is usually a chasm. A brilliant paper from researchers at Oxford, BlackRock, and Chicago Booth has pulled back the curtain, and it is the ultimate BS-detector for anyone working in quant, asset management, or fintech.
The Paper

'Evaluating LLMs in Finance Requires Explicit Bias Consideration' by Yaxuan Kong et al. (arXiv:2602.14233, February 2026). The authors—including Stefan Zohren from Oxford and Alejandro Lopez-Lira from Florida—reviewed 164 academic and industry papers on financial LLMs published between 2023 and 2025. Their conclusion? Almost all of them are reporting spectacular, but completely fake, results because they violate basic rules of financial backtesting.
The Five Sins of Financial LLMs

The authors identify five recurring biases that systematically inflate the reported performance of financial LLMs, making them look like genius investors on paper when they are actually just cheating:

items: Look-Ahead Bias (The Time Machine): The model uses information that was not available at decision time. This often happens because the LLM's pre-training cutoff date includes the backtest period. If you ask a model trained in 2025 to 'predict' stock moves in 2024, it isn't predicting; it's just remembering what it already read on the internet.

Survivorship Bias (The Ghost Town): The evaluation universe silently drops companies that went bankrupt, merged, or got delisted. If your LLM is only backtested on today's S&P 500, it looks brilliant because it never had the chance to buy Enron or Lehman Brothers.

Narrative Bias (The Storyteller): LLMs are literally built to write plausible, beautiful stories. In finance, they will happily force highly noisy, random market data into a clean, convincing narrative that sounds incredibly smart but has zero actual predictive power.

Objective Bias (The Confident Idiot): The model is optimised for text-based metrics (like sentiment classification accuracy) rather than actual financial objectives (like risk-adjusted returns or portfolio variance). This leads to models that are highly confident but financially disastrous.

Cost Bias (The Free Lunch): Assuming zero transaction costs, zero slippage, and zero market impact. In the real world, trading costs and execution friction easily wipe out any theoretical alpha, especially for high-turnover LLM strategies.

content.text: The Killer Stat & Quote

The most damning finding in the paper is how oblivious the research community is to these issues. Out of the 164 papers reviewed, not a single bias was discussed in more than 28% of the studies. Most shockingly, survivorship bias was only mentioned in a measly 1.2% of papers. The authors do not mince their words about what this means for real-world deployment:
if any requirement fails, the reported result can only support a stress test interpretation or a proof of concept, and it cannot support a claim of deployable alpha.
How to Use This at Work (and in Interviews)

This paper is incredibly useful. If you are a quant or data scientist, it gives you a rigorous 'Structural Validity Framework' to audit your own models. If you are a PM, analyst, or VP, it is your shield against bad research. Next time a vendor or a junior analyst pitches an AI-driven trading strategy, you can politely dismantle their pitch by asking these questions over a coffee:

items: How did you control for pre-training leakage? If the LLM's weights were updated on data from our backtest period, how do we know it's not just memorising historical returns?
Does the backtest universe include delisted and bankrupt companies, or are we looking at a clean, survivorship-biased dataset?
What is the breakeven transaction cost for this strategy? If we factor in realistic slippage and execution lag, does the alpha survive?

content.text: The Sharpe Pint Verdict

This is a highly refreshing dose of cold water on the AI-in-finance hype. The City is full of people trying to sell 'GPT-powered hedge funds,' but most of them are just rediscovering look-ahead bias with a fancy API. This paper should be mandatory reading for every quant desk in London. Skim the literature review, but spend your time on Section 2 (the five biases) and Section 3 (the evaluation checklist). It will save you millions of pounds and a lot of embarrassment.

sections.title: People / Business Psychology: The Decoy Effect

content.text: The Decoy Effect: How to make a £120k fee look like a bargain

If you have ever stood in a London pub trying to decide between a mediocre £6.80 pint of lager, a £7.90 craft IPA, and an absurd £9.50 double-dry-hopped stout, you have likely fallen victim to the Decoy Effect. You probably did not want to spend nearly ten pounds on a single drink, but suddenly that £7.90 IPA looked like a sensible, mid-tier compromise. In reality, the pub owner priced that £9.50 stout specifically to make you buy the £7.90 IPA.

In psychology and behavioural economics, this is known as the Decoy Effect (or the Asymmetric Dominance Effect). First formally documented by academics Joel Huber, John Payne, and Christopher Puto in 1982, it describes how people's preferences between two options change dramatically when they are presented with a third, strategically flawed option—the decoy.

Human brains are notoriously bad at valuing things in a vacuum. We do not know what a 'fair' price for an advisory mandate, a software license, or a bottle of wine is until we compare it to something else. The decoy exploits this weakness by being 'asymmetrically dominated': it is completely inferior to one option (the target) but only slightly inferior to the other (the competitor), making the target look like an absolute steal.
Imagine you are pitching an asset management mandate or a corporate advisory fee structure to a client. If you give them two choices, they will agonise over the price jump:

items: Option A (The Budget): Basic execution, standard quarterly reporting. Price: £50,000.
Option B (The Target): Full execution, bespoke structuring, 24/7 team access. Price: £120,000.

content.text: Many clients will default to Option A because £120,000 feels like a massive leap. To fix this, you introduce the decoy:

items: Option C (The Decoy): Full execution, bespoke structuring, 24/7 team access, plus a quarterly 'strategic dinner' with the senior partner. Price: £175,000.

content.text: Option C is priced aggressively high for very little extra utility (unless the client is desperate for rubbery chicken and awkward small talk with a partner who wants to catch the 8:15 train back to Surrey). Suddenly, Option B is no longer 'the expensive option'. It is 'the smart option'—you get 95% of the value of the premium package while saving £55,000. The client happily signs off on the £120,000 fee, feeling like they have outsmarted your pricing committee.

You can use this in your daily work life, especially when managing upwards. If you want your VP or Managing Director to sign off on a specific analytical approach or model structure, do not just present your favourite. Present three options: a basic, underwhelming one (Option A); your preferred, well-rounded, robust model (Option B); and an incredibly complex, resource-heavy option that takes three times as long for marginal extra gain (Option C). By framing your preferred path next to an over-engineered monster, you make the sensible choice look like the only logical path forward.
To make your preferred option look like an absolute bargain, always bring along a slightly worse, overpriced friend.

stuff_worth_remembering: US-Iran peace talks have sent Brent crude tumbling over 4% to around $95.52, easing global inflationary pressures.
Uber launched a €11.5bn bid for Delivery Hero, signaling massive consolidation in the food delivery space.
SpaceX filed its S-1 for a historic Nasdaq listing, targeting a $1.75tn valuation despite a $4.9bn loss in 2025.
UK M&A activity has tripled to $192bn in 2026 as foreign buyers aggressively exploit the persistent FTSE valuation discount.
Fed Governor Waller warned that the central bank's easing bias is dead, keeping rate hikes on the table if inflation remains sticky.
